ia-support.label: IA & support N1
ia-support.rule: Un signal IA ET un contexte support ou exploitation. « IA », « AI » ou « Claude » ne comptent que dans le titre.

acces.label: Accès & authentification
acces.rule: Un motif fort, ou un motif faible (GPO, TLS, certificats, hameçonnage) dans le titre ou avec un autre motif. Les formules qui décrivent une faille (« sans authentification », « contournement de l'authentification »…) et les faux amis (« certificats médicaux », « photo d'identité ») sont retirées avant la recherche.

outils.label: Outils du support
outils.rule: Article qui cite GLPI ou Request Tracker, outils de support utilisés en stage, ou nouvelle version de ces outils (préversions ignorées).

alerte.label: Alerte CERT-FR
alerte.rule: Toute alerte du CERT-FR est gardée, même hors des deux thèmes : une alerte concerne toujours un administrateur.

items.text: Today we’re announcing the public preview of Microsoft Entra Conditional Access policy plans —a new framework for enterprise-scale access control. Instead of managing dozens of individual policies, policy plans let you define your access intent once and enforce it consistently across every identity. Scale and control are now complementary, not mutually exclusive. This evolution moves Conditional Access from administrative configuration toward policy management without sacrificing granularity or manageability. It helps identity teams close coverage gaps faster, improve policy clarity, and bring emerging identity types, such as AI agents, into the same trusted model. Policy plans run side by side with your existing Conditional Access policies, so you can start with one plan and expand from there. Check out this Microsoft Mechanics video for a first look at Conditional Access policy plans in Microsoft Entra and see the latest features in action. How it works Let's start with what a policy plan is. A policy plan groups related Conditional Access policies around one security objective, such as requiring compliant devices or securing agent activity. Every plan has three parts: Part What it is What it enables Plan details Name, description, optional tags, and owners. Clear accountability. Identity admins can see what the plan is for, who owns it, and what a change could affect. Shared conditions Targeting you define once for the whole plan, such as users in scope and emergency…

items.text: Employees, and now AI agents, need secure access to resources wherever they live: the internet, Microsoft 365 and SaaS, cloud and datacenter workloads, on-premises apps, and AI services. Zero Trust means evaluating every one of those connections against full context, including identity, risk, device, app and data, location, and network, and enforcing the decision continuously, not only at sign-in. Organizations need to do that without stitching together separate tools and policies. Today, we’re taking the next step in our Secure Access Service Edge (SASE) journey: customers can now purchase Microsoft Entra Private Access and Microsoft Entra Internet Access together as a single Microsoft Entra Glo bal Secure Access offering. This is not a new product; it’s a simpler way to purchase these capabilities together. Microsoft Entra Private Access and Microsoft Entra Internet Access will also continue to be available individually. How Microsoft Entra Glo bal Secure Access fits Microsoft Entra Glo bal Secure Access offering , available starting November 2, 2026, is for organizations that want identity-aware network access for private and internet traffic as a unified offering. items.title: AI agents are coming—are your identity controls prepared?
items.excerpt: AI is reshaping identity risk. Attackers now use AI to automate phishing, social engineering, and privilege escalation, making credential theft faster and more convincing than ever. SMS codes and push approvals can be…
items.text: AI is reshaping identity risk. Attackers now use AI to automate phishing, social engineering, and privilege escalation, making credential theft faster and more convincing than ever. SMS codes and push approvals can be intercepted, while standing privileges give attackers reach far beyond a single account. On the other hand, as organizations adopt AI agents, identity risk grows exponentially. Securing agent identities is critical to maintaining trust and control. The same principles that protect user identities must now extend to every agent identity. Reinforcing the principles Microsoft’s recently published guidance, Secure identity to get ready for AI , reinforces key principles for securing identities: move users and administrators to phishing-resistant multifactor authentication (MFA), eliminate standing privileges with Microsoft Entra Privileged Identity Management (PIM), and extend a unified policy engine to govern every identity. Putting the principles into practice Implement these principles in sequence to strengthen your Zero Trust foundation and secure every identity, starting with the accounts and controls you already manage: Move users and admins to phishing-resistant MFA. Protect privileged accounts first by requiring MFA for every administrator and moving them to device-bound passkeys or FIDO2 security keys. Plan a phishing-resistant, passwordless authentication rollout across your workforce using methods such as Windows Hello for Business, device-bound…

items.title: How are you using ChatGPT for everyday IT tasks? Sharing my prompt structure
items.excerpt: Hi everyone, I’m new to the community. I’ve been experimenting with using ChatGPT to speed up routine IT work, and I’ve found that the quality of the answer depends almost entirely on how the prompt is written. A…
items.text: Hi everyone, I’m new to the community. I’ve been experimenting with using ChatGPT to speed up routine IT work, and I’ve found that the quality of the answer depends almost entirely on how the prompt is written. A structure that works well for me: Role: “Act as a Windows sysadmin with 10 years of experience.” Task: “Write a PowerShell script to list all users who haven’t logged in for 90 days.” Context: “Active Directory environment, Windows Server 2019.” Format: “Give the script, then a short explanation of each section.” Limits: “Don’t make changes, read-only output only.” Where it has saved me time: Drafting helpdesk replies and user instructions Writing first-draft documentation and SOPs Explaining error messages in plain language Generating script outlines (always tested in a lab first) A caution: never paste passwords, internal IPs, or customer data into public AI tools, and always review anything before running it in production. Curious how others here are using AI at work: What tasks do you trust it with, and which ones do you avoid? Does your company have a policy on AI tools? 11 posts - 11 participants Read full topic

items.title: Why identity needs network insight to make Zero Trust work
items.excerpt: Your users sign in successfully—and then what? The session can be hijacked, device posture can degrade, and traffic to non-federated SaaS and AI apps can slip past the identity controls you trust to protect them.…
items.text: Your users sign in successfully—and then what? The session can be hijacked, device posture can degrade, and traffic to non-federated SaaS and AI apps can slip past the identity controls you trust to protect them. That’s the gap admins see every day: identity tells you who, but not what’s happening across the network during the session—and it’s why identity alone can’t carry Zero Trust on its own. Most Zero Trust strategies start with identity—and for good reason. Identity is the control point for authenticating users and granting access. But identity by itself can’t address every evolving risk. Today, users connect from anywhere, on any device, and interact with thousands of apps across cloud, AI, internet, and private networks. The gap between identity and network security creates blind spots that attackers can exploit. Microsoft’s approach is clear: identity is most effective when it operates with full awareness of the network. That’s why Microsoft Entra brings identity and network protections together in a unified architecture designed for modern Zero Trust security. Why identity alone is not enough Traditional access decisions often stop at sign-in and rely on credentials plus multifactor authentication. This works for many scenarios—but not all. In practice, a session that looks low-risk at sign-in can turn risky minutes later, and unmanaged traffic to AI tools and non-federated SaaS apps creates blind spots your identity policies weren’t designed to cover Why? items.title: Designing smarter access policies for hybrid enterprises
items.excerpt: Every hybrid enterprise eventually reaches the same point: the security model that worked when everyone was inside the corporate network no longer holds up when people, apps, and data are distributed across clouds,…
items.text: Every hybrid enterprise eventually reaches the same point: the security model that worked when everyone was inside the corporate network no longer holds up when people, apps, and data are distributed across clouds, data centers, and unmanaged devices. Add AI agents acting on users’ behalf, and the idea of a trusted perimeter loses even more relevance. The answer is not more controls for their own sake, but better-designed policies: deliberate rules that determine who and what can access specific resources, under which conditions, and how access adapts as risk changes. Get the design right, and security becomes an enabler rather than a burden. Get it wrong, and you either leave gaps attackers can exploit or frustrate the users you are trying to protect. This article explains how to get it right. TL;DR In a hybrid enterprise, users, apps, and data no longer sit behind a single perimeter, and AI agents also make access requests. This article explains how to design Microsoft Entra Conditional Access policies and policy governance for that reality, protecting what matters without slowing people down. The goal is a Zero Trust posture you can operate, not merely deploy. Why this matters Hybrid work is no longer a transition state; it is the operating model. Most organizations now run apps across multiple clouds, maintain legacy systems on-premises, and support a distributed workforce that expects access to feel immediate and seamless. That combination creates real tension in…

items.text: Today’s highlights cover two pressing issues: Shelby Green discusses Microsoft Teams and the threat of deepfakes , noting that while Microsoft is implementing detection tools to combat AI impersonation in meetings, IT departments must still enforce strong verification protocols for sensitive requests since technology can have its flaws. Meanwhile, Rose de Fremery sheds light on OAuth phishing , where attackers are cleverly circumventing multi-factor authentication by deceiving users into allowing harmful apps access to their email. It’s crucial to regularly audit app permissions and educate teams on recognizing fraudulent consent screens. That wraps up today’s articles! items.text: This is a security release, upgrading is recommended Warning Important note: with the upcoming release of GLPI 12.0.0, version 10.0.28 will be the final release of the 10.0 branch, which will no longer receive bugfixes. This release fixes a few security issues that have been recently discovered. Update is recommended! You will find below the list of security issues fixed in this bugfixes version: [SECURITY - High] Authorization bypass in massive actions [SECURITY - High] Privilege escalation via user cloning [SECURITY - High] Improper rights checks in users deletion [SECURITY - High] SQL Injection through form actors dropdown [SECURITY - Medium] Users names enumaration via the planning feature [SECURITY - Medium] Missing authorization checks in the planning feature Many bug fixes have also been made, read the full changelog is available for more details. We would like to thank all people who contributed to this new version and all those who contributes regularly to the GLPI project! Regards.

items.title: GLPI 12.0.0
items.excerpt: We are proud to announce the official release of GLPI 12 , the latest major version of our open-source software. After months of development and community testing, GLPI 12 is now stable and ready for production. What’s…
items.text: We are proud to announce the official release of GLPI 12 , the latest major version of our open-source software. After months of development and community testing, GLPI 12 is now stable and ready for production. What’s new ? While the full list of changes can be found in the detailed changelog , here are some of the most important highlights: 📖 Knowledge base - full rewrite : An overhaul for pretty dated feature in GLPI, the whole frontend of the integrated knowledge system has been rewritten from scratch to give you a modern experience. 🛡️ Session Management : GLPI records every session opened on the instance. As an administrator you can now see who is currently signed in and revoke any session. 🔓 Step-Up Authentication : Some administrative actions now ask you to prove it is still you. ⏱️ Group-managed OLAs : They are now mutliple and are tied to a group. 🧑‍🦯 Accessibility : GLPI makes a first pass on accessibility, following RGAA and RAWeb criteria. The work will continue over the coming releases. Get Started with GLPI 12 Today You can download the new stable release here: 📦 GLPI 12 Archive 🐳 Official Docker Image Documentation , To match the GLPI 12.0 release, the user documentation has been fully rewritten. What’s Next? In the coming months, we’ll continue to: Monitor feedback and release patches when needed. Expand integrations and plugins to enrich the ecosystem. Explore new innovations to keep GLPI a modern, reliable ITSM platform. A huge thank you to our community…

items.title: What’s new in Microsoft Entra: October 2026
items.excerpt: Over the last few months, I've spent a lot of time with customers and our teams on one of the biggest security shifts ahead of us: securing an enterprise where people and AI agents are both acting on behalf of the…
items.text: Over the last few months, I've spent a lot of time with customers and our teams on one of the biggest security shifts ahead of us: securing an enterprise where people and AI agents are both acting on behalf of the business. It’s a challenge shaping Microsoft's approach to Secure AI. And while AI makes the challenge urgent, the underlying problem is broader. Organizations need to give more people, applications, workloads, and agents access to more resources, while maintaining control without adding more friction and complexity. Identity and network access are at the center of the transition. Customers are clear about what they need. Across my conversations with identity and network access leaders and practitioners, and through our ongoing customer research, four outcomes consistently rise to the top: Keep my organization trusted and resilient Give users and agents secure access without friction Reduce the cost and complexity of access management Adopt AI safely at enterprise scale So, we're making a change to this blog. Starting this month, we’re organizing “What’s New” around the outcomes you're trying to achieve, rather than around our product architecture. Our goal is to make the connection between what we're shipping, the challenges you’re having, and where we're headed much clearer. I welcome your feedback on this new approach in the comments. items.excerpt: Many IT service desks are buried in password resets and status requests, and the usual response is a full ITSM platform migration. Aditya Santhanam argues for a cheaper route: wrap conversational AI around the ITSM…
items.text: Many IT service desks are buried in password resets and status requests, and the usual response is a full ITSM platform migration. Aditya Santhanam argues for a cheaper route: wrap conversational AI around the ITSM tool you already run, so AI agents work inside existing records, SLAs, and rules. The article covers seven use cases, a six-step rollout, what to keep humans on, and the metrics that show it works.
